sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Gronw ​Pebr** (*gronwpebr*) ‌— Gronw ‌the Strong ​· Gronw ​the strong ​— belongs ​to the ​Celtic tradition, ‌where it ​is ​catalogued under ‌the domain ​"Lover of ‌Blodeuwedd". The ​name means ‌"Gronw the ​strong"[^1].

**Gronw ​Pebr** is ​the Mabinogi’s ​tragic ​villain: the ‌lord of ​Penllyn who ‌loved Blodeuwedd, ​the wife ‌fashioned of ​flowers for ‌Lleu Llaw ​Gyffes, ‌and who ​— guided ​by her ‌— cast ‌the spear ‌that could ​kill the ​seemingly invulnerable ‌hero through ​the ​bath-house wall. ‌The Fourth ​Branch’s justice ​is symmetrical ‌and severe: ​Lleu’s return, ‌Gronw’s plea, ​and the ​stone that ​still ​bears the ‌mark of ‌the spear ​he asked ‌to be ​placed between ​himself and ‌the fatal ‌throw.[^2]

PuniCodex ‌restores ‌the name ​as **Gronw ‌Pebr** and ​serves its ​temple at ​[its temple](https://punicodex.com/gronwpebr/). ‌The restoration ​aSCII-equivalent form ​— ​a description ‌computed from ​the displayed ​form itself. ​The plain ‌ASCII form ​*gronwpebr* survives ‌as a ​modern convenience ‌imposed ​by the ‌early domain-name ‌system; the ​restoration, not ​the fallback, ​is the ​form the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
No ​indigenous written ‌attestation ‌survives for ​this ​name; **Gronw ​Pebr** ​is a ​scholarly ‌transliteration of ​the ​reconstructed spoken ‌form. ​Etymologically the ‌name ​means "Gronw ‌the ​strong"[^1].

The ​ASCII ​form *gronwpebr* ​survives ​only because ‌the ​early domain-name ‌system ​could not ‌carry ​diacritics; it ‌is ​a technological ‌compromise, ​not an ​ancient ‌spelling. The ‌Unicode ‌restoration **Gronw ​Pebr** ​recovers the ‌full ​diacritic detail ​of ‌the scholarly ​transliteration ​directly in ‌the ​address bar. ‌The ​restoration aSCII-equivalent ​form ​— a ​description ‌computed from ‌the ​displayed form ‌itself.

​The letter-by-letter ​transformation ‌runs:

- **g** ‌→ ‌**G** — ‌Same, ​capitalized
- **r** ‌→ ​**r** — ​Same
- ​**o** → ‌**o** ​— Same
- ​**n** ​→ **n** ‌— ​Same
- **w** ​→ ​**w** — ‌Same
- ​**p** → ‌**P** ​— Same, ‌capitalized
- ​**e** → ‌**e** ‌— Same
- ​**b** ​→ **b** ​— ​Same
- **r** ‌→ ‌**r** — ​Same

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of ‌the name ​is ​**/ˈɡrɔnuː ˈpɛbr/** ​— ​Middle Welsh ​(normalised).[^1]

‌Phoneme by ​phoneme:

- ​**Gronw** — ‌Welsh; ​the w ‌is ​a full ‌vowel ​(“oo”), so ​the ​name is ​“GRON-oo”.
- ​**Pebr** — ‌“The Strong” ​— ‌pebyr/pebr is ​the ‌epithet; the ​compound ‌means Gronw ​the ‌Strong.
- **** ​— ​The name ‌survives ‌in the ‌Fourth ​Branch of ​the ‌Mabinogi, the ​Math ​fab Mathonwy ‌cycle.

​For the ​modern ‌speaker, the ​closest ‌approximation is: ​“GRON-oo ​PEBR” — ​two ​words, the ‌second ‌meaning “the ​strong”

‌Kindred and ​historical ​forms of ‌the ‌name:

- **Epithet** ‌— ‌Gronw Pebyr ​— ‌the fuller ​spelling ​of “the ​strong”
- ‌**Cycle** — ​the Fourth ​Branch ​of the ‌Mabinogi ​(Math fab ​Mathonwy)

​His story ‌is ​the Mabinogi’s ‌darkest: ​the lover ‌who ​killed Lleu ‌Llaw ‌Gyffes with ​the ​only spear ​that ​could, cast ‌through ‌a bath-house ​wall.

sections.body:
**Gronw ​Pebr** is ‌the Mabinogi’s ‌tragic villain: ​the lord ​of ​Penllyn who ​loved Blodeuwedd, ​the wife ‌fashioned ​of flowers ​for Lleu ‌Llaw Gyffes, ​and who ‌— ​guided by ‌her — ​cast the ​spear that ​could ​kill the ​seemingly invulnerable ‌hero through ​the ‌bath-house wall. ​The Fourth ‌Branch’s justice ​is symmetrical ‌and ​severe: Lleu’s ‌return, Gronw’s ​plea, and ​the ‌stone that ‌still bears ‌the mark ​of the ​spear ‌he asked ​to be ​placed between ‌himself and ​the ​fatal throw.[^1]

### ‌The Spear

​He cast ‌the ​year-wrought, dawn-forged ​spear through ​the bath-house ​wall — ‌the ‌only weapon ​that could ‌wound Lleu.

### ​Blodeuwedd

The ​flower-wife ‌he loved ‌— her ‌name means ‌“flower-face”; ​their plot ‌killed her ​husband.

### The ​Bath-House

The ​one ‌door through ​which Lleu ​could be ​killed: ‌standing with ​one foot ​on bath ​and one ‌on ​goat-skin, spear ‌through the ​wall.

### The ‌Stone

His ​last ‌plea: a ‌stone between ​himself and ​Lleu’s ​return-cast — ​the spear ‌went through ‌it, and ​him.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated ‌with Gronw ​Pebr ​concentrates ​in ​a ​small set ‌of ​recurring ​attributes, ‌each ​a ‌compressed statement ​about ‌the ​name:[^1]

- ​**The ​Spear** — ​He ​cast ‌the ​year-wrought, ‌dawn-forged ​spear through ‌the ​bath-house ‌wall ​— ‌the only ​weapon ​that ‌could ‌wound ‌Lleu.
- ​**Blodeuwedd** — ​The ‌flower-wife ​he ​loved ‌— her ​name ​means ‌“flower-face”; ​their ‌plot ​killed her ​husband.
- ​**The ​Bath-House** ‌— ‌The one ​door ‌through ​which ​Lleu ‌could ‌be killed: ‌standing ‌with ​one ‌foot ​on bath ​and ​one ‌on ​goat-skin, ​spear ​through the ‌wall.
- ​**The ​Stone** ​— ‌His last ​plea: ‌a ​stone ‌between ​himself ‌and Lleu’s ‌return-cast ​— ​the ​spear ​went through ‌it, ‌and ​him.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Gronw’s mythology ​is the Fourth Branch’s ‌dark triangle: the man, ‌the flower-wife, and the ​hero engineered to be ​unkillable. The Mabinogi tells ​it without relish and ​without excuse — ​the one Welsh narrative ‌in which adultery, murder, ​and retribution each get ​exactly their due, and ‌the landscape itself (the ​Cynfael river, the stone ‌at the bank) keeps ​the receipt.[^1]

### The ‌Flower-Wife’s Plot (Math fab ​Mathonwy)

Blodeuwedd, made of ​flowers by Gwydion and ​Math for the cursed ​Lleu, met Gronw by ​the Cynfael and loved ‌him. Her husband’s ​invulnerability had one precise ‌condition — he could ​be killed only while ‌standing with one foot ​on a bath and ‌one on a goat-skin, ​and only by ‌a spear worked a ​year at the dark ​of the moon. She ‌persuaded Lleu to demonstrate ‌the posture; Gronw waited ‌behind the bath-house wall ​with the finished spear.[^2]

### ​The Cast Through ‌the Wall (Math fab ​Mathonwy)

The cast went ​through the wall and ‌through Lleu, who changed ​into an eagle and ​vanished into the forest. ‌Gronw took Blodeuwedd ​and Lleu’s lands. But ‌Lleu was found, healed ​by Gwydion’s wizardry, and ​returned in a year’s ​turning — the cursed ​hero restored by the ‌uncle whose flower-magic ‌had made the wife ​who betrayed him.

### The ‌Stone of the Return-Cast ​(Math fab Mathonwy)

The ​law of the tale ‌is exact symmetry. Gronw ‌offered compensation — land, ‌gold, any price ‌— and Lleu refused ​all but one thing: ‌the return-cast. Gronw’s single ​plea was granted: a ​stone between him and ​the spear. The cast ‌went through the ​stone and through Gronw, ​and the stone stood ​by the Cynfael for ‌centuries as the tale’s ​material proof — the ​Mabinogi’s most literal monument.

### ​The River Cynfael’s ‌Mark (Landscape Tradition)

Welsh ​tradition placed the story ‌in the real country ​of Penllyn and the ‌river Cynfael — the ​spear-stone was shown to ‌travellers as a landmark, ‌the narrative pinned ​to the map like ​a deed. The Mabinogi’s ​habit of grounding its ​marvels in named places ‌makes Gronw’s story the ‌Welsh myth-cycle’s most topographically ​anchored tragedy.

sections.label: Irish Mythological Cycles
sections.body:
The Irish mythological cycles — the Mythological, Ulster, Fenian, and Historical Cycles — preserve Gronw Pebr in medieval manuscript tradition. Texts such as Lebor Gabála and the Táin Bó Cúailnge place the figure within Irish cosmogony and heroic narrative.

The restored form Gronw Pebr follows normalized Old/Middle Irish orthography.[^1]

sections.label: Welsh Sources
sections.body:
Welsh medieval sources, including the Mabinogion and Welsh Triads, preserve cognate or parallel traditions to Gronw Pebr. These prose tales rework older Celtic material for a Welsh literary audience.

The Unicode restoration Gronw Pebr preserves the scholarly spelling.[^1]

sections.label: Inscriptions & Seals
sections.body:
Inscriptions in Ogham and Latin script occasionally preserve names and epithets from the Celtic world. While direct attestations of Gronw Pebr are rare, the epigraphic habit confirms the figure's place in the broader insular Celtic landscape.

The restored form Gronw Pebr serves as the modern scholarly anchor.[^1]
